title: The Useless Wood of the Vine
overview: Through a short picture about vine wood, Ezekiel warns the people still in Jerusalem that their city will not escape being destroyed by Babylon.

parts.label: A question about vine wood (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Older poems pictured Israel as the LORD's treasured vine, so listeners may have expected praise, but Ezekiel asks only about the wood. Vine wood is thin and twisted, too weak even to make a peg for hanging a pot, so it is worth less than the wood of any ordinary tree.

parts.label: Burned at both ends (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: If the wood was useless when whole, it is even more useless once fire has charred both ends and the middle. Many interpreters read the burned ends as earlier disasters to the nation and the burning middle as Jerusalem, now under attack, though the text does not say this outright.

parts.label: Jerusalem thrown in the fire (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: God says he will treat Jerusalem's people like that wood and will "set my face against them," meaning he will turn firmly against them. The people who survived one fire are probably those left in the city after Babylon's first attack in 597 BC, warned that a worse one is coming, which happened when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC.

parts.label: The reason given (v. 8)
parts.note: The land will be left empty because the people broke faith with God, a word used for betraying a trust, like breaking a sworn agreement. Ezekiel blames the ruin on that betrayal, not on Babylon's strength or on bad luck.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the fire here means only the historical fall of Jerusalem, or also points beyond it to a final judgment, a link some draw through Jesus' words about branches thrown into the fire in John 15.
think: Is there something you have counted on to keep you safe, such as a name, a history, or a place you belong, and how would you know whether it could really hold up?
